teile.einleitung: ‘A Theory of Justice’ is the main work of the American philosopher John Rawls. The book appeared in 1971 and asks according to which principles a just society should be built.
wichtigste: John Rawls published ‘A Theory of Justice’ in 1971.
He sums up his theory as ‘justice as fairness’.
In the **original position**, free and equal people choose the principles of justice.
Behind the **veil of ignorance** nobody knows their future position.
Equal basic liberties for all have priority.
The difference principle only allows inequality if it benefits the least well-off most.
In 1974 Robert Nozick criticised Rawls from a libertarian point of view.

abschnitte.text: **John Rawls** lived from 1921 to 2002 and taught at Harvard University. His book **‘A Theory of Justice’** appeared in 1971 and greatly revived political philosophy. In German it is called ‘Eine Theorie der Gerechtigkeit’. Rawls sums up his theory with the slogan **‘justice as fairness’**. He deliberately sets it against **utilitarianism**, which only looks at the greatest total benefit.

Rawls carries out a thought experiment. In the **original position**, people are to choose the rules of their society. They are free, equal and rational. But they are behind a **veil of ignorance**: nobody knows their background, talents, wealth or future position. So nobody chooses rules that favour only themselves. The principles are fair because they are chosen under fair conditions.

The **first principle** guarantees everyone an equal system of **basic liberties**, such as freedom of opinion and freedom of conscience. This principle has **priority** over all others. Basic liberties must not be restricted just to gain economic advantages. The second principle also demands **fair equality of opportunity** in access to offices and positions.

According to the **difference principle**, inequalities in income and wealth are only allowed if they benefit the **least advantaged** the most. So a doctor may earn more if this benefits everyone, including the poorest. Why choose this way? According to Rawls, in the original position people use the **maximin rule**: you choose the option whose worst outcome is the best. If you do not know where you will end up, you protect yourself against the worst fate.

Rawls's theory was widely discussed. **Robert Nozick**, a colleague at Harvard University, criticised it in 1974 in ‘Anarchy, State, and Utopia’ from a **libertarian** point of view. He defended a minimal state and saw redistribution through taxes as an intrusion into property rights. Others thought that Rawls demanded too little equality. To this day the book is a basic text of political philosophy.

gewusst: As a young soldier, John Rawls served in the Pacific in the Second World War.
‘A Theory of Justice’ has been translated into many languages.

teile.einleitung: Everyone sometimes makes mistakes or hurts others, often without meaning to. With an apology you show that you are sorry and clear the way for making up.
wichtigste: You apologise even for an accident.
A good apology includes admitting the mistake.
A real apology has no ‘but’.
You can also make up for damage you have caused.
It is best to apologise as soon as possible.
Forgiving means letting go of your anger.

abschnitte.text: If you bump into someone by accident, you say: ‘Sorry!’ That way the other person knows it was **not on purpose**. An apology shows that the other person matters to you. It helps make sure that nobody stays angry or sad for long. It is best to apologise **as soon as possible**; then the anger passes more quickly.

In a good apology you say **what you did wrong**. For example: ‘I'm sorry I knocked over your tower.’ You look at the other person and mean it honestly. A bad apology would be: ‘Sorry, but it's your fault.’ Anyone who blames the other person in the same sentence is not really apologising. A real apology has **no ‘but’**.

You can also show an apology through actions. If you build a knocked-over tower back up, you **make amends** for the damage. If you have damaged a book, you can help to mend it. That shows you mean it. Words and actions together are often the best apology.

When someone apologises to you, you can say: ‘That's all right, thanks.’ Anyone who **accepts** an apology ends the quarrel. **Forgiving** means no longer holding the mistake against the other person and letting go of your anger. That does both of you good. Sometimes you need a little time for this, and that is fine.

When two people are friends again after a quarrel, this is called **making up** or reconciliation. It often begins with an apology. Afterwards you can play and laugh together again. Quarrels are part of life. What matters is learning how to end them again.

gewusst: The German word ‘Entschuldigung’ actually means freeing someone from their guilt.
In everyday life in Switzerland people also often say ‘Exgüsi’, which comes from the French ‘excusez’.

teile.einleitung: Ethics is a branch of philosophy. It asks what good and right action is and how moral rules can be justified.
wichtigste: The word ethics comes from the Greek ‘ethos’, meaning habit, custom and character.
Aristotle made ethics a subject in its own right.
Morality is the practice people live by; ethics thinks about it.
Descriptive ethics describes morality without judging it.
Metaethics examines the meaning of moral statements.
Applied ethics includes, for example, medical, business and environmental ethics.
According to David Hume, an ought does not automatically follow from an is.

abschnitte.text: The word **ethics** comes from the Greek **‘ethos’**. It refers to a person's usual dwelling place, their customs and their character. **Aristotle** is regarded as the founder of ethics as a field of its own. He treated it as a separate discipline alongside logic and physics. His well-known work is called the ‘Nicomachean Ethics’.

In philosophy a distinction is often made between **morality** and **ethics**. Morality is the norms and values a community actually lives by, for example ‘You should not steal’. Ethics is **thinking about morality**. It asks why a rule applies and whether it is well justified. In everyday life, however, the two words are often used to mean the same thing.

**Descriptive ethics** describes which moral ideas apply in a society, without judging them. It works rather like sociology or ethnology. **Normative ethics** asks what we should do. Important approaches are virtue ethics, the ethics of duty and consequentialist ethics. **Metaethics** stands one level above: it examines what words such as ‘good’ mean and whether moral statements can be true.

**Applied ethics** transfers ethical theories to concrete areas of life. These include **medical ethics**, **business ethics** and **environmental ethics**. Typical questions are about fair wages, protecting nature or how we treat animals. In Switzerland, for example, the National Advisory Commission on Biomedical Ethics advises the authorities and the public on human medicine.

In the 18th century the Scottish philosopher **David Hume** noticed that many authors switch from ‘is’ to ‘ought’ without realising it. But an ought does not simply follow from statements about what is. This is called the **is-ought problem**. Another disputed question concerns **ethical relativism**. It says that moral norms only apply relative to a culture. Critics object that then you could no longer condemn, for example, slavery in other cultures.

gewusst: Aristotle was a pupil of Plato and the teacher of Alexander the Great.
The ‘Nicomachean Ethics’ is probably named after Nicomachus, the son or father of Aristotle.
